episode_title: Ep. 49 | How Agentic AI Will Rebuild Insurance Operations with Kyle Nakatsuji, Founder of ClearCover

real_qa.q: Why did Kyle Nakatsuji found Dearborn Labs after 10 years building ClearCover?
real_qa.r: When Anthropic rolled out Opus 6 in January and 45 products in 45 days, Nakatsuji and his co-founder realized that the technology was capable of end-to-end reasoning and solving complex problems at a level far beyond previous iterations. They concluded that knowing what this technology was capable of, everything at ClearCover would have to change. Even as a 10-year-old tech-native insurer and early AI adopter, they would have to start from scratch, leading them to create Dearborn Labs to help the industry navigate this transformation.
real_qa.requete: Why did Kyle Nakatsuji start Dearborn Labs

real_qa.q: What are the four common failure modes of AI implementations in insurance businesses?
real_qa.r: The first is consultants delivering slideware instead of software—100-slide presentations without implementation capability. The second is bolting AI on top of existing workflows not designed for it, adding AI costs without reducing expenses or capturing its full potential. The third is buying platforms when building custom technology would deliver better outcomes, especially now that development costs have changed. The fourth is spending too much on large horizontal platforms and not enough on vertical applications that generate immediate ROI, making the platform investment unrecoverable.
real_qa.requete: Four common failure modes AI insurance implementations

real_qa.q: How should insurers architect AI-native operating models with legacy systems like Guidewire and Duck Creek?
real_qa.r: Data availability is the first consistent theme—determining where data lives in the business and making it available to new tools in the required format, particularly when data lives on mainframe or during cloud migration. The second is building a contextual layer between AI implementations and the underlying data systems. Rather than having agents work from policy admin documentation alone, they need access to the actual context of how decisions are made operationally—such as underwriting decisions made in Slack DMs—so agents can replicate human decision-making accurately.
real_qa.requete: AI architecture legacy insurance systems Guidewire Duck Creek

real_qa.q: What is the difference between building great AI implementations and over-building them?
real_qa.r: Great AI implementations often have less AI than people think. The fastest way to make them work badly is to put AI in processes that should be deterministic and automated in the first place. Instead, you must map workflows to determine where AI needs to exist—where decisions require probabilistic reasoning—versus where deterministic logic suffices. Putting AI only where decisions require reasoning, combined with hooks and deterministic steps, creates more consistent and reliable systems than letting AI run loose on entire processes.

real_qa.q: How can agents detect early warning signs of loss ratio deterioration in insurance operations?
real_qa.r: Rather than waiting for frequency trends by coverage, insurers can look at mix of business—whether they are binding the mix expected based on pricing. Going even earlier, they can monitor bind rate; when bind rate suddenly exceeds expected levels, it often signals a hole in pricing discovered by distribution channels. In an agentic world, a distribution agent can instantly alert the claims agent that bind rate increased unexpectedly in a particular channel or state, triggering immediate investigation without waiting for cross-functional meetings.
real_qa.requete: Detect loss ratio warning signs insurance bind rate

guest.bio_context: Kyle Nakatsuji spent a decade building ClearCover, a tech-enabled insurer founded on the thesis that building from scratch using available technology could create better customer experiences and advantaged cost structures. Before ClearCover, he worked as a lawyer and venture investor with American Family. In January 2025, he co-founded Dearborn Labs with ClearCover's former COO to help other insurers rebuild their operations for the AI era, after realizing that even a decade-old native insurer built for technology must be fundamentally reconstructed to leverage modern agentic AI capabilities.
